name: Wendy Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run Brookside, a hundred and twenty hectares of organic veg, laying hens and outdoor pigs, owned by an older couple, the Morlands. We pack about two thousand veg boxes a week for people in the city. My morning is the hens first, then a planning chat with the AI about what's ready to pick, then I'm out with the crew. I've got eight people in summer, four in winter.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said a planning chat with the AI. What does that look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every morning I tell it what's in the ground, the weather and the box orders, and it gives me a picking plan and flags anything that's going to bolt. It's wrong maybe one day in ten, and I can spot that. Last summer we trialled a little solar weeding robot in the carrots, which the crew named Gerald. My partner Callum is a paramedic, and he thinks I love Gerald more than him some weeks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd say I was a bit disappointed. I'd post something about how the hype outran the tech, but the useful bits are still useful. The picking plans alone save me an hour a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I keep doing my job the way I'm already doing it, with a few clever tools. That's fine for me. What bothers me more is that farm pay stays rubbish for my crew, and AI was never going to fix that, only politics could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using what works, and probably buy a second weeding robot if the Morlands agreed, because Gerald paid for himself in hand-weeding hours. I'd keep pushing for a pay rise for the crew, maybe a pound an hour more. Our savings would just keep ticking along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a little sigh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Gerald paid for himself. Did anyone lose hours because of him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One seasonal weeder got six fewer weeks. I gave her those hours on the packing line instead, so it came out even. But I noticed it, and I'd be lying if I said I didn't think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the next year look like in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same rhythm. Hens, plan, pick, pack. Asha would be starting secondary school, and Ben would still be begging to drive the quad. I'd be quite happy with that, really.

S0.say: I'd post that the hype outran the tech but the useful bits stay useful, since the picking plans alone save me an hour a day. I'd admit I was a little disappointed.
S0.think: I keep doing my job the way I already do, with a few clever tools, which suits me. What bothers me is that farm pay stays low for my crew, and only politics can fix that.
S0.do: Keeps using the tools that work and asks the Morlands to buy a second weeding robot, since the first paid for itself. Pushes for about a pound an hour more for the crew while savings tick along.
S0.feel: Calm, with a small sigh of disappointment.
S0.quote: What bothers me more is that farm pay stays rubbish for my crew, and AI was never going to fix that, only politics could.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy is the rare farmer who is a little disappointed by the plateau. She already uses AI daily and has trialled a weeding robot, but she watches its effect on her crew closely. Her politics show in seeing pay as a political problem rather than a technical one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to decide who gets the gains. If robots do the weeding and picking, the people who used to do it should share in what's saved. I'd say it at the organic growers' meeting and probably write a long post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think this is great for me. I'm the one on the farm who already knows the tools, so I become more valuable, not less. The crew's the problem. Half of them are seasonal, and seasonal work is what goes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get two or three more robots in, for weeding and maybe harvesting salad. I'd train two of the permanent crew to run and fix them, at a higher rate. And I'd go to the Morlands with an idea I've had for a while: turn Brookside into an employee-owned farm when they retire, so the crew owns the robots too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, honestly, with a bit of guilt underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned guilt. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the seasonal pickers. Some of them have come back every year for six years. I can tell myself it's new jobs, it's fairer, but they'd still be the ones not getting the call in April.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you think the Morlands would take the employee ownership idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Morland would say it's a hippie scheme. Mrs Morland would ask for the numbers. I'd bring the numbers, and I'd use the AI to build them, which would annoy him even more.

S1.say: I'd tell the organic growers' meeting and post online that this is the moment to decide who gets the gains. People whose work the robots take should share in what's saved.
S1.think: I think this is good for me, because I already know the tools and become more valuable. The seasonal crew is the problem, since seasonal work goes first.
S1.do: Brings in two or three more robots for weeding and salad harvesting, and trains two permanent crew to run and fix them at a higher rate. Proposes to the Morlands that Brookside become employee-owned when they retire, so the crew owns the robots too.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, with guilt underneath.
S1.quote: They'd still be the ones not getting the call in April.
S1.fieldNote: Wendy sees steady change as an opening for herself and does not hide it. Her guilt about the returning seasonal pickers is real and specific. Her answer to the gap is ownership: she wants the crew to own the machines rather than be replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that two years is too fast for anyone to share anything, and that the government should tax the robot owners to pay people while they adjust. I'd be posting every day, probably. I'd be one of those people at the town hall with a microphone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately? Two years is the one that scares me even though I like the tech. If AGI can plan the farm better than me, my edge is gone. I'm good because I'm early with the tools, and in two years everyone's early, because the tools do it all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd get the Morlands to buy whatever's best before the price goes up, and I'd make sure I'm the one setting it up. We'd put an extra four hundred a month into savings and drop the holiday to Callum's sister's. And I'd start talking to the robot companies, because if they need people who know how real farms work, I want to be first in that queue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My head is racing, but it's the kind of race where I still feel like I'm steering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your edge is being early. What's left if everyone is early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knowing the land. Knowing that the bottom field floods every February and the hens hate the north wind. Maybe that's worth something to a robot company for a year or two. After that, I don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Callum's work? Does that change things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot. Robots won't be doing ambulance runs in two years, I don't think, so his pay is our floor. That's the thing that stops this being panic. I'd hate to be relying on him, though. I've always paid my half.

S2.say: I'd post every day and take the microphone at the town hall to say two years is too fast to share anything. The government should tax robot owners to pay people while they adjust.
S2.think: Two years scares me even though I like the tech, because my edge is being early with tools. If the tools do everything, everyone is early and the edge is gone.
S2.do: Gets the Morlands to buy the best kit early and sets it up herself, adds four hundred a month to savings and drops the holiday to Callum's sister's. Approaches robot companies to work for them as someone who knows real farms.
S2.feel: Anxious, with a racing head, but still feeling she is steering.
S2.quote: I'm good because I'm early with the tools, and in two years everyone's early, because the tools do it all.
S2.fieldNote: Being an early adopter doesn't protect Wendy in the fastest picture, and she sees that sharply. Her partner's paramedic job is what keeps her from panic, though she dislikes depending on him. She would move towards the robot makers rather than away from them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to build the rules properly: a robot tax, worker ownership, retraining. And I'd say farms are a good place to try it, because the work is visible and everyone eats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for me to get Brookside ready. I think I'd turn it into a showcase farm, robots doing the field work, people doing the selling, the teaching, the animal care. I'd still be needed, just in a different chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd write the plan for employee ownership and get the crew to vote on it. I'd take an online course in robot maintenance, because nobody local can fix Gerald when he breaks. By year three we'd run farm visits for schools, and that's a side income that robots can't really do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly hopeful, but it's a lot of moving parts to get right in five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots can't really do school visits. Are you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'm not sure. A robot could probably talk to the kids. But parents want to see a person who's had muck under their nails. At least I hope they do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomasz, who's been here nine years and does the hens. He's careful and slow, and he hates screens. I'd want to make sure the hens stay a person's job as long as possible, for him.

S3.say: I'd say we have five years to build the rules properly, with a robot tax, worker ownership and retraining. Farms are a good place to try it because the work is visible and everyone eats.
S3.think: Five years is enough to get Brookside ready as a showcase farm, with robots in the fields and people doing the selling, teaching and animal care. I'd still be needed, just in a different chair.
S3.do: Writes an employee ownership plan in year one and gets the crew to vote on it, and takes an online robot maintenance course. By year three starts school farm visits as a side income.
S3.quote: But parents want to see a person who's had muck under their nails. At least I hope they do.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Wendy's ideas into a timetable. She admits she isn't sure the visitor business is robot-proof. She wants to protect the hen work for a long-serving worker who struggles with screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if we use it. Every farm worker should get paid training, and every farm that buys robots should give the crew a share. I'd be saying that everywhere I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is fine for me. I'm fifty-three then, and I'd have had a decade of running robots before most people start. The worry is whether the rules arrive in time for the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, just faster. More robots, more training for the crew, employee ownership done by year four. I'd also sit on the county farming board, because that's where the rules get shaped.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. This is the one where I can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said calm. Is there anything in this picture you'd lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The summer mornings out with eight people picking, laughing, Tomasz telling the same jokes. If the robots pick and the crew run them from the shed, that goes. I'd miss it more than I'm admitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Asha and Ben about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the job you start with won't be the job you finish with, and that's all right. And that if you can, own a slice of the thing you work on. That's the bit I wish someone had told me.

S4.say: I'd say everywhere I could that ten years is a gift if we use it. Every farm worker should get paid training and every farm that buys robots should give its crew a share.
S4.think: Ten years is fine for me, since I'd have run robots for a decade before most people start. My worry is whether the rules arrive in time for the crew.
S4.do: Speeds up what she already does: more robots, more crew training and employee ownership finished by year four. Joins the county farming board to help shape the rules.
S4.feel: Calm, because she can see the road ahead.
S4.quote: If you can, own a slice of the thing you work on. That's the bit I wish someone had told me.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Wendy expects to do well and puts her energy into the crew and the rules. Asked what she'd lose, she named the shared summer picking and admitted she was underplaying it. Her advice to her children is about ownership more than skills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, which surprises me, because I'm the robot person. What would help is a tax on the robot owners that pays people while they find their feet, and a law that makes it easy for a crew to buy into the farm they work on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the animals and the soil. A robot that weeds carrots is great. A robot told to squeeze every last penny out of a field will wreck it. Someone has to set the goals, and I'd want it to be people who love the place.

headlineQuote: A robot told to squeeze every last penny out of a field will wreck it.
portrait: Wendy Patel is 43 and runs Brookside, an organic veg, egg and pig farm that packs two thousand boxes a week, with a crew of four to eight. She plans each day with an AI tool, trialled a weeding robot the crew named Gerald, and believes the real question is who owns the machines. She is calm about the plateau and steady change, which she sees as good for her, but anxious about two-year AGI because her edge of being early would vanish, with her partner's paramedic pay as the family's floor. With five or ten years she plans employee ownership, school visits and a seat on the county farming board, while quietly mourning the summer mornings picking with her crew.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, which surprises her, because in two years everyone's tools catch up and her head start disappears.
whatWouldHelp: A tax on robot owners that pays people while they adjust, and a law that makes it easy for a crew to buy into the farm they work on.
